test.title: Mathematics 1 Calibration

student_intro.heading: Find your starting level
student_intro.supportingText: Some questions reward a quick observation more than a long calculation. If you get stuck, make your best choice and keep moving.

instructions: Choose one answer for every question.
Diagrams are not intended to be measured.
Do not show difficulty, answer, scoring, or inspiration metadata during the test.
research_design_notes: Every item should have a short exact solution and at least one useful observation.
Do not require the quadratic formula; discriminant reasoning is permitted.
Avoid extended algebraic expansion, repetitive arithmetic, and measurement from diagrams.
Use difficult items to reward structural insight rather than syllabus obscurity.
Use diagrams only when they carry mathematical information.
test.originality_statement: Questions are original or substantially transformed ESAT CAMP items. Historic NSAA papers informed pacing and reasoning mechanisms only; no official wording or numerical construction is reproduced.

score_model.method: MAP 3PL item-response estimate on a fixed theta grid
score_model.mappingRationale: The official score scale fixes the cohort median at 4.5 and the 90th percentile at 7.0. The mapping treats theta 0 as the intended calibration-cohort median and theta 1.2816 as its 90th percentile.
displayRules: Label the output 'Estimated ESAT range', never 'Official ESAT score'.
Show the posterior 16th-84th percentile interval rounded outward to 0.1.
Do not narrow the displayed interval below 0.8 score points before empirical calibration.
Always show raw score alongside the estimate.
Timing affects pace feedback, not the estimated score.
If fewer than 12 questions are answered, show 'Not enough evidence' instead of a score.
score_model.recalibrationRequirement: After at least 200 serious completions, fit item difficulty and discrimination to response data. Link the ESAT scale only when matched official-score data or an equivalent defensible external anchor is available.

questions.question_text_markdown: \(ABCD\) is a square of side \(12\text{ cm}\). The points \(E,F,G,H\) are the midpoints of its sides. A circle touches all four sides of the square \(EFGH\). What fraction of the area of \(ABCD\) lies inside the circle?
questions.diagram_alt_text: A square ABCD of side 12 centimetres. Its side midpoints E, F, G and H form a rotated inner square, and a circle is inscribed in that inner square.
questions.fast_insight: The inner square's diagonal is the outer square's side.

solution.title: The inner square's diagonal is the outer square's side.
steps_markdown: The diagonals of \(EFGH\) are both \(12\), so its side is \(6\sqrt2\). The circle therefore has radius \(3\sqrt2\) and area \(18\pi\). Since \(ABCD\) has area \(144\), the fraction is \(18\pi/144=\boxed{\pi/8}\).

questions.pair_interpretation: Same curriculum area (M1-M5) across different presentations.

questions.question_text_markdown: What is the exact value of \[\frac{1}{\sqrt5-2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt5+2}?\]
questions.fast_insight: The two denominators are conjugates whose product is 1.

solution.title: The two denominators are conjugates whose product is 1.
steps_markdown: Since \((\sqrt5-2)(\sqrt5+2)=1\), the two reciprocals are \(\sqrt5+2\) and \(\sqrt5-2\). Their difference is therefore \((\sqrt5+2)-(\sqrt5-2)=\boxed4\).
solution.final_answer_markdown: Since \((\sqrt5-2)(\sqrt5+2)=1\), the two reciprocals are \(\sqrt5+2\) and \(\sqrt5-2\). Their difference is therefore \((\sqrt5+2)-(\sqrt5-2)=\boxed4\).

questions.fast_insight: Collect every term containing q before dividing.

solution.title: Collect every term containing q before dividing.

questions.question_text_markdown: Two different numbers are chosen at random from \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). What is the probability that their product is divisible by \(6\)?
questions.fast_insight: A successful product needs both a factor 2 and a factor 3; list unordered pairs rather than 36 ordered rolls.

solution.title: A successful product needs both a factor 2 and a factor 3; list unordered pairs rather than 36 ordered rolls.
steps_markdown: There are \(\binom62=15\) unordered pairs. The successful pairs are \((1,6),(2,3),(2,6),(3,4),(3,6),(4,6),(5,6)\): seven pairs. The probability is \(\boxed{7/15}\).

questions.question_text_markdown: \(ABCD\) is a square of side length \(1\). Points \(P,Q,R\) lie on \(AB,BC,CD\) respectively. \[AP:PB=1:2,\qquad BQ:QC=1:3,\qquad CR:RD=1:1.\] What is the area of triangle \(PQR\)?
questions.diagram_alt_text: A unit square ABCD. P divides AB in the ratio 1 to 2, Q divides BC in the ratio 1 to 3, and R is the midpoint of CD. Triangle PQR is shaded.
questions.fast_insight: The region to the left of PR is a trapezium; subtract it and the two corner triangles from the square.

solution.title: The region to the left of PR is a trapezium; subtract it and the two corner triangles from the square.
steps_markdown: Subtract the three surrounding regions from the square. Triangle \(PBQ\) has area \(\tfrac12(2/3)(1/4)=1/12\). Triangle \(QCR\) has area \(\tfrac12(3/4)(1/2)=3/16\). Quadrilateral \(ADRP\) is a trapezium with parallel sides \(AP=1/3\) and \(DR=1/2\), so its area is \(\tfrac12(1/3+1/2)=5/12\). Therefore \[1-\frac1{12}-\frac3{16}-\frac5{12}=\boxed{\frac5{16}}.\]

questions.pair_interpretation: Same curriculum area (M1-M5) across different presentations.

questions.question_text_markdown: The line \(y=2x+5\) touches the curve \(y=x^2-4x+k\) at exactly one point. What is the value of \(k\)?
questions.fast_insight: Exactly one intersection means a repeated root, so set the discriminant to zero.

solution.title: Exactly one intersection means a repeated root, so set the discriminant to zero.
steps_markdown: At an intersection, \(x^2-4x+k=2x+5\), so \(x^2-6x+k-5=0\). Touching once means the discriminant is zero: \[(-6)^2-4(k-5)=0.\] Hence \(36-4k+20=0\), giving \(\boxed{k=14}\).

questions.question_text_markdown: The positive integers are arranged in a square spiral as shown. The pattern continues in the same way. Which number is directly below \(100\)?
questions.diagram_alt_text: The integers 1 to 25 are shown on a five-by-five square spiral. One is at the centre, two is immediately right of it, and the spiral turns anticlockwise. The pattern continues beyond 25.
questions.fast_insight: Track the odd-square corners rather than extending the whole spiral to 100.

solution.title: Track the odd-square corners rather than extending the whole spiral to 100.
steps_markdown: The odd squares \(81=9^2\) and \(121=11^2\) are successive lower-right corners. The next layer runs from \(82\) up the right edge and then left along the top edge. This places \(100\) one square above the top-left corner of the \(9\times9\) layer. That corner contains \(81-16=65\), so the number directly below \(100\) is \(\boxed{65}\).

questions.question_text_markdown: For every real value of \(x\), \[F(x)=3^{x^2-8x+18}.\] What is the smallest possible value of \(F(x)\)?
questions.fast_insight: Minimise the exponent; there is no need to sketch or differentiate the exponential.

solution.title: Minimise the exponent; there is no need to sketch or differentiate the exponential.
steps_markdown: Complete the square in the exponent: \[x^2-8x+18=(x-4)^2+2.\] Its minimum is \(2\), reached when \(x=4\). Therefore the smallest value is \(3^2=\boxed9\).
solution.final_answer_markdown: Complete the square in the exponent: \[x^2-8x+18=(x-4)^2+2.\] Its minimum is \(2\), reached when \(x=4\). Therefore the smallest value is \(3^2=\boxed9\).

questions.question_text_markdown: The line \(AT\) is tangent to the circle at \(A\). Points \(A,B,C\) lie on the circle, \(AB=AT\), and \(\angle ATB=70^\circ\). What is \(\angle ACB\)?
questions.diagram_alt_text: A circle passes through A, B and C. AT is tangent at A. Triangle ABT is outside the circle, AB and AT are equal, and angle ATB is 70 degrees.
questions.fast_insight: Use the isosceles triangle first, then transfer its remaining angle with the tangent-chord theorem.

solution.title: Use the isosceles triangle first, then transfer its remaining angle with the tangent-chord theorem.
steps_markdown: Since \(AB=AT\), triangle \(ABT\) is isosceles, so \(\angle ABT=70^\circ\). Hence \(\angle BAT=40^\circ\). By the alternate segment theorem, the angle between tangent \(AT\) and chord \(AB\) equals \(\angle ACB\), so \(\boxed{40^\circ}\).

questions.question_text_markdown: Two gears mesh without slipping. The smaller gear has \(18\) teeth and makes \(25\) complete revolutions in \(12\) seconds. The larger gear has \(30\) teeth. How many complete revolutions does the larger gear make in \(1\) minute?
questions.diagram_alt_text: A small gear with 18 teeth meshes with a larger gear with 30 teeth. The small gear is labelled 25 revolutions in 12 seconds.
questions.fast_insight: Count teeth passing the contact point; the two gears pass the same number of teeth.

solution.title: Count teeth passing the contact point; the two gears pass the same number of teeth.
steps_markdown: In \(12\) seconds the small gear moves \(25\times18=450\) teeth past the contact point. The large gear therefore makes \(450/30=15\) revolutions. One minute is five lots of \(12\) seconds, so it makes \(5\times15=\boxed{75}\) revolutions.

questions.question_text_markdown: Bag \(A\) contains two red counters and one blue counter. Bag \(B\) contains one red counter and two blue counters. One counter is chosen at random from Bag \(A\) and transferred to Bag \(B\). A counter is then chosen at random from Bag \(B\), and it is red. What is the probability that the transferred counter was red?
questions.diagram_alt_text: Bag A contains counters R, R and B. Bag B contains counters R, B and B. An arrow shows one unknown counter moving from Bag A to Bag B before a counter is drawn from Bag B.
questions.fast_insight: Compare the two routes that can produce the observed red counter.

solution.title: Compare the two routes that can produce the observed red counter.
steps_markdown: A red transfer followed by a red draw has probability \((2/3)(2/4)=1/3\). A blue transfer followed by a red draw has probability \((1/3)(1/4)=1/12\). Given that the draw is red, the required probability is \[\frac{1/3}{1/3+1/12}=\boxed{\frac45}.\]

questions.question_text_markdown: A square and a regular hexagon are inscribed in two circles of equal radius. What is \[\frac{\text{area of the regular hexagon}}{\text{area of the square}}?\]
questions.diagram_alt_text: Two equal circles are shown side by side. A square is inscribed in the first and a regular hexagon is inscribed in the second.
questions.fast_insight: An inscribed regular hexagon splits into six equilateral triangles whose side equals the radius.

solution.title: An inscribed regular hexagon splits into six equilateral triangles whose side equals the radius.
steps_markdown: Let the common radius be \(r\). The square has diagonal \(2r\), so its area is \(2r^2\). The hexagon is six equilateral triangles of side \(r\), so its area is \(6(\sqrt3 r^2/4)=3\sqrt3 r^2/2\). The ratio is \[\frac{3\sqrt3 r^2/2}{2r^2}=\boxed{\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}}.\]

questions.fast_insight: Rewrite the requested expression before trying to solve for x.

questions.question_text_markdown: Two runners start a race at the same time and run at constant speeds. Runner \(A\) runs \(25\%\) faster than Runner \(B\). At one instant, Runner \(A\) has \(80\text{ m}\) left and Runner \(B\) has \(140\text{ m}\) left. How long is the race?
questions.fast_insight: At the same instant, distance travelled has the same ratio as speed—not distance remaining.

solution.title: At the same instant, distance travelled has the same ratio as speed—not distance remaining.
steps_markdown: Let the race length be \(L\). At the stated instant, the distances run are \(L-80\) and \(L-140\). Since the runners have travelled for the same time, \[\frac{L-80}{L-140}=\frac54.\] Thus \(4L-320=5L-700\), giving \(\boxed{L=380\text{ m}}\).

questions.question_text_markdown: Three circles of radii \(1\text{ cm}\), \(4\text{ cm}\), and \(9\text{ cm}\) rest on the same straight line. Each circle touches the next circle. The points where the circles touch the line are \(P,Q,R\), as shown. What is \(PR\)?
questions.diagram_alt_text: Three circles of radii 1, 4 and 9 centimetres rest on a horizontal line and touch consecutively. Their points of contact with the line, from smallest to largest circle, are P, Q and R.
questions.fast_insight: Join neighbouring centres: the horizontal gap is the missing side of a right triangle.

solution.title: Join neighbouring centres: the horizontal gap is the missing side of a right triangle.
steps_markdown: For two touching circles of radii \(a\) and \(b\), their centres are \(a+b\) apart and differ in height by \(b-a\). Their horizontal separation is therefore \[\sqrt{(a+b)^2-(b-a)^2}=2\sqrt{ab}.\] Hence \(PQ=2\sqrt{1\cdot4}=4\) and \(QR=2\sqrt{4\cdot9}=12\). Therefore \(PR=4+12=\boxed{16\text{ cm}}\).

diagnostic_model.scope_note: This calibration diagnoses Mathematics 1 only. Physical reasoning is not scored; it should be reported as not_applicable rather than inferred from mathematical performance.
diagnostic_model.weighted_accuracy_formula: 100 * sum(difficulty_weight * correct) / sum(difficulty_weight) over the score's evidence questions
diagnostic_model.confidence_calibration_formula: 100 - 25 * mean(abs(predicted_probability - correctness)), where confidence 1..5 maps to probabilities 0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.95; clamp to 0..100

calculation_accuracy.calculation: 100 * (weighted correct answers not tagged as concept_gap or wrong_method) / weighted attempted answers; use observed error attribution when available, otherwise weighted accuracy

time_management.calculation: 0.65 * mean pace_score_per_question + 0.20 * completion_rate + 0.15 * end_section_completion_rate, where end_section is questions 11-15

consistency.calculation: 100 - 12.5 * unexplained_pair_disagreements - 5 * high_confidence_reversals; clamp to 0..100. A disagreement is not penalised when the harder item is wrong and the pair interpretation identifies a narrower skill.

confidence_calibration.reliability: high if at least 12 confidence ratings, medium if 7-11, low if 1-6

reliability_rule.high: at least 4 relevant questions or at least 3 relevant questions with one deliberate pair
reliability_rule.insufficient: 0 relevant questions or more than half the relevant questions skipped

diagnostic_model.overclaiming_guardrail: Never describe a low-reliability score as a stable weakness. Use 'possible weakness' and recommend confirmation with additional questions.

rules_in_priority_order.label: clear_knowledge_gap
rules_in_priority_order.condition: weighted_accuracy <= 40 and relevant_attempted_questions >= 2 and (slow_wrong_count >= 1 or high_confidence_wrong_count >= 1)

rules_in_priority_order.label: inconsistent
rules_in_priority_order.condition: all remaining cases with at least 2 evidence questions

profile_classification_rules.label: Broadly ready
profile_classification_rules.condition: overall_readiness >= 75 and completion_rate >= 0.9 and no high-reliability skill score < 60

profile_classification_rules.label: Strong in familiar problems, weaker in unfamiliar contexts
Needs foundational work
profile_classification_rules.condition: overall_readiness < 45 and knowledge < 50 and at least 4 curriculum tags have weighted_accuracy < 50

strong_but_slow.reason_template: Accuracy is secure, but median response time is above the target range.

fast_but_inaccurate.reason_template: Responses are faster than target but error rate is too high.
fast_but_inaccurate.reassessment_condition: after 40 attempts with at least 80% accuracy

developing.reason_template: Understanding is partial but not yet reliable across contexts.

clear_knowledge_gap.reason_template: Repeated errors indicate a concept or method gap rather than pace alone.
clear_knowledge_gap.reassessment_condition: after completing the topic lesson and 30 practice questions

inconsistent.reason_template: Performance changes substantially across closely related questions.
inconsistent.reassessment_condition: after 2 mixed sets with no repeated error pattern

insufficient_evidence.reason_template: The calibration did not collect enough relevant evidence.
insufficient_evidence.reassessment_condition: after at least 5 additional questions in this skill

strong_and_fast.reason_template: Accuracy and speed are both currently strong.
strong_and_fast.reassessment_condition: reassess in 21 days or after a performance drop

result_page_schema.suggested_retest_date_rule: 7 days for fast-but-inaccurate or strong-but-slow profiles; 10-14 days for developing or clear knowledge gaps; 21 days for broadly ready profiles
result_page_schema.precision_warning: This 15-question calibration provides directional evidence. Low-reliability conclusions must be confirmed with more questions.
